I picked **candidate 0**. I worked this out in my head without running a simulation, and the choice between candidates 0, 2 and 3 is close.

1. **The days that can't be helped are the same for everyone.** An order takes 5 days to arrive, so on days 1–4 there will be shortages and penalties under every plan. That doesn't separate the candidates.

2. **Ordering every day wastes money.** Candidate 5 places 25 orders, which is about 1350 in per-order fees. The every-other-day plans place 13 orders, about 702. Candidate 5 gets nothing in return for the extra roughly 650.

3. **Every third day hits the warehouse limit.** Candidate 6 brings in about 130–146 units at a time, plus whatever is left over. That is close to the 152-unit limit, so some stock gets thrown away when it arrives. It also needs more safety stock, because each order has to cover a longer stretch.

4. **Candidates 0–4 differ only in size.** They are the same every-other-day plan, scaled to roughly 1.0× (4), 1.1× (1, 3), 1.15–1.2× (0) and 1.25–1.3× (2) of the forecast. Candidate 7 has the same structure, shifted by one day, at about 1.1×.
   - A shortage costs about 16 per unit for product 0 and about 15 for product 1 (lost margin plus penalty). An excess unit costs only holding at first, because shelf life (6 and 8 days) is longer than the 2-day cycle, so leftovers carry over.
   - Demand is random, so stock drifts. At about 1.05–1.1× (candidates 1, 3, 4, 7) the cushion builds too slowly and shortages stay frequent, given the actual average demand is about 1.046× the forecast.
   - At about 1.25–1.3× (candidate 2) stock builds steadily. That leads to spoilage, product 0 costing 11 per unit, and to arrivals of up to about 137 plus leftovers going over the 152 limit, mainly on days 9, 11 and 27.
   - Candidate 0, at about 1.15–1.2×, keeps a working cushion with only moderate spoilage. I expect it to have the highest profit.

I picked **candidate 7**, based on a rough hand simulation using forecast demand rather than an exact calculation. What decides it is the cash shortfall in the first days.

- **Unavoidable early losses.** No order arrives before day 5. The starting stock (22 and 34 units) runs out after 1–2 days. On days 1–4 every plan pays about 1,000 in penalties, so cash falls close to zero or below.
- **Candidates 0–4** order every two days and differ only in scale. Their large orders on days 0 and 2 drain the cash, so the day-4 order gets cut short: product 1 gets nothing and product 0 gets only part. That causes stockouts on days 9–10, then cut and cancelled orders on days 6, 12 and 14. The cycle is still going on day 18, when cash is only about 1,070 for candidate 4. The larger versions (0, 2, 3) do worse.
- **Candidate 5** places a small order every day. That costs about twice as much in 54-per-order fees, and it still gets cut and cancelled on days 4–6 and 11–12. There are still stockouts on days 16–17.
- **Candidate 6** places large orders every three days. In this rough check it hits the same cash cutbacks as candidates 0–4, and with deliveries of up to 146 units at once it also risks going over the 152-unit warehouse limit.
- **Candidate 7** starts with a small order on day 0 and moves the large orders to odd days. It loses only the day-5 order and has a short dip around days 10–12. After that it fully recovers: by day 18 it has about 2,360 in cash, about twice as much as candidate 4. From there the plan runs as written.

Я выбрал **кандидата 0**. Это оценка в уме, я ничего не моделировал, поэтому разница между близкими кандидатами не гарантирована.

1. **Кандидаты 0–4 — один и тот же план.** Заказ раз в 2 дня, разница только в запасе сверх прогноза: 4 — 1,0×; 3 — 1,1×; 0 — 1,15×; 1 — 1,2× в начале, 1,05× в середине, 0,95× в конце; 2 — 1,25×.
2. **Нехватка обходится дороже излишка.**
   - Товар 0: нехватка стоит 16 за единицу (8 упущенной маржи + 8 неустойки), излишек — не больше 11 (закупка, если партия испортится) плюс хранение. Выгодно закрывать около 59 % вероятных значений спроса.
   - Товар 1: нехватка стоит 15 (7 + 8), излишек — около 5. Здесь лучше закрывать около 75 %.
   - Остатки не пропадают сразу, а продаются в следующие дни, пока не истечёт годность (6 и 8 дней), так что излишек обходится ещё дешевле. Значит, стоит заказывать с запасом заметно выше прогноза.
3. **Почему не меньше 1,15×.** Средний множитель спроса около 1,046. При 1,0× (кандидат 4) заказ в среднем ниже спроса, а при 1,1× (кандидат 3) запас прибавляет всего около 2 единиц за цикл при разбросе около 8. Кандидат 1 в середине срока заказывает 1,05×, то есть примерно по среднему спросу, и под конец 0,95×. Значит, на большей части срока он будет недобирать.
4. **Почему не больше 1,15×.** При 1,25× (кандидат 2) копятся остатки товара 0, который портится через 6 дней. Кроме того, около дней 9–10 есть риск переполнить склад на 152 места.
5. **Остальные хуже по устройству.**
   - Кандидат 5 заказывает каждый день и платит 54 за заказ 25 раз.
   - Кандидат 6 заказывает раз в 3 дня крупными партиями, а значит, больше риск переполнения склада и больше расходы на хранение.
   - Кандидат 7 почти такой же, как 3, только на нечётные дни и с лишним заказом в день 0.

Заявленные авторами итоги (4700–5300) я не проверял и при выборе на них не опирался.

I picked **Candidate 3**, but I didn't simulate the plans; this is a rough estimate. The authors' claimed results can't be trusted, so I set them aside. With random demand, Candidates 0, 1, 3 and 7 could come out in a different order.

1. **Shortages can't be avoided on days 0–4 under any plan.** The first orders only arrive on day 5. Starting stock is 22 of product 0 against about 80 forecast demand, and 34 of product 1 against about 109. The early penalties are roughly the same for every candidate.
2. **Ordering every 2 days beats the alternatives.** Daily orders (Candidate 5) pay the 54 fee 25 times. Ordering every 3 days (Candidate 6) runs into the 152-unit warehouse limit and costs more in holding.
3. **The safety margin needs to be above 1.0.** A missing unit costs about 16 for product 0 (lost margin 8 plus penalty 8) and about 15 for product 1. Leftover units mostly roll into the next cycle, because shelf life (6 and 8 days) is longer than the 2-day cycle. Overstock costs holding fees and some write-offs, at most 11 or 5 per unit. A newsvendor-style estimate puts the best margin at roughly 1.05–1.15 × forecast.
4. **Ruling out the extremes:**
   - Candidate 4 orders exactly the forecast. Since average demand is about 4.6% above forecast, stock keeps drifting down and penalties pile up.
   - Candidate 2 orders at 1.25×. The day-9 delivery of 137 units plus leftover stock is likely to overflow the warehouse, and more goes to waste.
   - Candidate 1 orders at about the true average demand in the middle of the horizon, so its stock just wanders randomly. Its early buffer runs out, and the 0.95× orders at the end add shortages.
5. **The remaining contenders are Candidates 3, 7 and 0.** Candidate 7 is the same 1.1× plan as Candidate 3, shifted to odd days, with the same number of orders, so I expect a nearly identical result. Candidate 0 at 1.15× is close behind, with a bit more write-off. I chose 3 because 1.1× sits in the middle of the estimated best range.

I picked **candidate 0** by estimating in my head, without simulating any plan.

1. **Candidates 0–4** follow the same pattern: an order every second day, with each delivery covering 2 days of demand. They differ only in scale. On the day-4 order (covers days 9–10, forecast 63 units of item 0), the ratios to forecast are about 1.14 for candidate 0, 1.05 for 1, 1.25 for 2, 1.10 for 3 and 1.00 for 4.
2. **The best ratio is above forecast.** The demand multiplier averages about 1.046, and its spread over 2 days is about 0.21 in log terms.
   - Item 0: a shortage costs 8 lost margin plus an 8 penalty, so 16. A spoiled unit costs 11. The best stock level is near the 59% point of demand, roughly 1.10× forecast.
   - Item 1: a shortage costs 7 plus 8, so 15. A spoiled unit costs 5. The best stock level is near the 75% point, roughly 1.19× forecast.
   - Leftovers carry over for 6 and 8 days, so overstocking costs less than this suggests. That favours about 1.15×, which matches candidate 0.
3. **Candidate 5** orders every day, which adds about 12 × 54 ≈ 650 in fixed order costs.
4. **Candidate 6** orders every 3 days. That saves about 216 in order costs, but single deliveries reach 144–146 units on top of leftover stock. With a 152-unit warehouse, some of each delivery will likely be lost.
5. **Candidate 7** is shifted by a day, has a smaller margin (about 1.1×) and places one more order.

I'd pick **candidate 0**. I worked this out in my head, as the task requires, so it's an estimate, not an exact simulation.

**How the plans differ.** Candidates 0–4 follow the same plan: order every other day (days 0 to 24), with each order arriving 5 days later and covering two days of demand. They differ only in how far each order exceeds forecast demand:

| Candidate | Order size vs. forecast |
|---|---|
| 4 | about 1.00× |
| 1 | about 1.05–1.10× |
| 3 | about 1.10× |
| 0 | about 1.15× |
| 2 | about 1.25× |

For example, candidate 0's day-0 order is 35 and 54, against forecast demand of 30 and 47 for days 5–6.

**Why about 1.15× is the best level.**
- **Stockouts cost more than leftovers.** A missing unit of item 0 loses 8 of margin plus an 8 penalty (16 total), while an extra unit costs 11. For item 1 it's 7 + 8 = 15 against 5. That favours ordering above forecast, especially for item 1.
- **Demand runs above forecast.** The multiplier averages 1.046, and two days of demand together vary by about ±21%. The best order level comes out around 1.10× for item 0 and about 1.19× for item 1. Candidate 0's 1.15× sits between them.
- **Extra stock usually isn't wasted.** Shelf life (6 and 8 days) is longer than the 2-day order cycle, so leftovers sell the next cycle and mostly cost only storage. That pushes the best level slightly higher still.
- **Candidate 2 overshoots.** Leftovers build up and run into the 152-unit warehouse limit, for example around the arrival on day 11.
- **The ending is handled.** Every plan in this group shrinks its last order (day 24), so little is left unsold on day 29.

**Why the other plans lose.**
- **Candidate 5** orders every day and pays the 54 fee 25 times, about 1,350, which eats most of the profit.
- **Candidate 6** orders every third day, so each batch is larger. Batches like that, plus leftovers, are more likely to hit the 152 limit, and item 0 has a higher chance of expiring.
- **Candidate 7** is similar to candidates 1 and 3, but it pays an extra order fee for a small day-0 order.

I picked **candidate 0**. This is an estimate worked out in my head, not a simulation, and it's close between candidates 0 and 3.

1. **Fewer order days is better.** Candidates 0–4 order every second day, which is 13 order days and about 700 in fixed fees. Candidates 5 and 7 order almost every day, so they pay up to about 650 more in fees for little gain.
2. **Candidate 6 risks spilling stock.** It orders every third day, in batches of up to 144 units. Added to what's already in stock, that can go over the 152-unit capacity, and the excess is lost after it has been paid for.
3. **Among candidates 0–4, order size is what differs.** Each one orders the forecast demand for the two days the delivery covers, multiplied by a factor:
   - candidate 4: about 1.0;
   - candidates 1 and 3: about 1.05–1.1 (candidate 1 varies more);
   - candidate 0: about 1.15;
   - candidate 2: about 1.25.

   A missed sale costs more than leftover stock:
   - **Product 0:** a missed unit loses 8 profit plus an 8 penalty. A leftover unit costs at most its purchase price of 11, and less if it sells before expiring.
   - **Product 1:** a missed unit loses 7 profit plus an 8 penalty. A leftover unit costs at most 5, and it keeps for 8 days, so it usually sells later.

   Real demand averages about 1.046 times the forecast. So the best factor is around 1.1–1.15, and higher for product 1. Candidate 0 fits that best. Candidate 2 orders too much: stock builds up and expires.

I estimated this in my head without running anything, so the choice is a judgement rather than a calculation. I'd pick **candidate 3**.

- **Fixed cost:** placing an order every 2 days costs 13 × 54. Candidate 5 orders daily (25 × 54), and candidate 7 places 13 orders while matching candidate 3's order sizes. Both pay more in fees for no extra benefit.
- **Order every 3 days (candidate 6):** this saves 4 × 54 = 216 in fees. Against that, it holds about 22 more units on average, costing roughly 340 in storage. It also cuts it close on the 152-unit capacity (144 units arrive on day 8 alone).
- **Same plan at different sizes (0–4):** candidates 0–4 follow the same 2-day pattern and differ only in how far above forecast they order: about 1.0× (4), 1.05× (1), 1.1× (3), 1.15× (0) and 1.25× (2). Any surplus carries over to later days until it expires, so the comparison is total stock against total demand over 6–8 days. Over that window the random swing shrinks to about 10–12%. Running short costs about 15–16 per unit (lost margin plus penalty). Over-ordering costs the purchase price plus storage, about 11+ for item 0 and about 8 for item 1. With those costs and an average multiplier of 1.046, the best target comes out at about 1.07–1.09× forecast. Candidate 3 is closest, and it orders a little high, which is the cheaper side to miss on. Candidate 2 at 1.25× would throw away about 20% of its purchases.

I picked **candidate 0**. I estimated this by hand, as the rules required, and did not simulate it, so treat the choice as a judgement call rather than a calculated result.

- **The first days are the same for every plan.** No order can arrive before day 5. The starting stock covers about one day, so all plans take the same shortages on days 1–4.
- **Storage space is not a problem for the every-2-days plans.** Stock peaks at about two days of demand plus a margin, which stays under 152. Plans 0–4 and 7 all place 13 orders, so their fixed order costs are almost the same. Candidate 5 orders every day (25 orders), and candidate 6 orders every 3 days, which means larger deliveries that risk going over 152 and more storage cost. Both start at a disadvantage.
- **A short sale costs more than a surplus unit.** For product 0, a missed sale costs 16 (lost margin 8 plus penalty 8) and a leftover unit costs 11 plus storage. For product 1, a missed sale costs 15 and a leftover costs only about 5. Both products favour ordering above forecast, product 1 much more so.
- **The safety margin is smaller than it looks.** Average demand is about 4.6% above forecast. Ordering at 1.1× gives only about 5% real extra stock, and ordering at exactly the forecast (candidate 4) runs short on average.
- **Surplus is not wasted quickly.** Products last 6 and 8 days, so extra units carry over to later days. That makes a bigger margin cheaper.

**Close call:** at 1.15× (candidate 0) versus 1.1× (candidate 3), I estimate an extra unit of product 0 sells before it expires well over 41% of the time. That is the point at which it pays for itself. For product 1 the higher margin is clearly better. So 1.15× should beat 1.1×. Candidate 2 at 1.25× probably goes too far, with more spoilage and storage cost.

I ignored the authors' claimed results because they are just their own numbers.

I pick **candidate 7**. My confidence is moderate: everything below is mental arithmetic on forecast (mean) demand, and storage costs are counted only roughly.

**What decides it is the cash shortage at the start.** Nothing ordered can arrive before day 5. The opening stock of 22 and 34 units is gone by day 1–2. From then until day 4 every plan pays penalties of roughly 330 per day. So the outcome depends on how each plan gets through running out of cash, not on how well its quantities match demand.

- **Candidates 0–4** are the same plan at different scales: an order every two days, each covering about 1.0–1.25× forecast demand. Each of them, after the day 0 and day 2 orders, has only 150–470 left on day 4. The day 4 order gets cut to a few units of product 0, and product 1 gets nothing (cuts hit product 0 first, even though product 1 earns more per unit spent). This falls into a repeating pattern: every other order is cut back or cancelled, followed by stretches of shortages and penalties.
  - Candidate 4 (the smallest): profit ≈ +290.
  - Candidate 2 (the largest): profit ≈ +1500.
  - Candidates 0, 1 and 3 behave the same way.
- **Candidate 5** orders every day, so it pays the 54 fee 25 times instead of 13. It also runs out of cash by day 4 and gets the same chain of cuts. I didn't trace it day by day.
- **Candidate 6** orders every three days. On day 3 its order loses almost all of product 1, and the day 6 and day 15 orders are cancelled for lack of money. The orders near 146 units are close to the 152-unit warehouse limit, so random swings risk spillover. Profit ≈ +2700.
- **Candidate 7** places a small order on day 0 and a large one on day 1. The day 5 order is cancelled, but the stock arriving on days 5–6 restores cash fast. After a partial cut on day 7 and a short gap on days 10–11, every order from day 9 on is paid in full. The orders made on day 21 and day 23 arrive on days 26 and 28, so the last days are covered too. Profit ≈ +4000 or more, even after allowing a few hundred for storage.

**Risk from random demand:** candidate 7's lead over the next best (6, then 2) is large. It also never comes close to the warehouse limit. I don't think an ordinary deviation from the forecast changes the ranking.

I picked **Candidate 0** by estimating in my head, without simulating any plan in full, so it's a judgement call. Candidate 3 is a close second.

1. **Cash is short early on for every plan.** The first deliveries only arrive on day 5. On days 0–4 you can sell only the starting 22 and 34 units, and the unmet demand costs about 330 in penalties per day. As a result, every plan's big orders on day 4–6 get cut down or cancelled for lack of money.
   - Candidate 7 orders heavily on days 1 and 3 and runs out of money. Its day-5 order is cancelled.
   - Candidate 5 orders every day, so it pays the 54 fee more often. Its day-5 order is also cancelled because orders are paid before that day's sales.
   - Candidate 6 orders every three days. Its day-6 order is cancelled entirely and its day-3 order of item 1 is heavily cut. Its large deliveries (up to 144 units at once) also risk overflowing the 152-unit warehouse.
2. **Candidates 0–4 are the same every-two-days plan at different sizes.** Candidate 4 is about 1.0× the forecast, Candidate 1 about 1.05×, Candidate 3 about 1.1×, Candidate 0 about 1.14× and Candidate 2 about 1.25×. Smaller plans keep a little more cash for the day-4 order, which is worth roughly 100–250. After day 8, cash stops being a constraint for all of them.
3. **A larger stock pays off over the remaining ~20 days.** True demand averages about 1.046× the forecast. A shortage costs more than a leftover unit: lost margin plus penalty is 16 for item 0 and 15 for item 1. A leftover costs at most the purchase price (11 and 5), and usually sells in the next cycle because shelf life is 6–8 days. I estimate the bigger buffer saves around 500 in shortages, which is more than the loss on the day-4 order. Candidate 2 goes too far: it loses even more on the day-4 order and risks overflow and spoilage.

On balance, Candidate 0 (about 1.14× the forecast) looks like the best compromise.

**Кандидат 7.** В уме я проследил подробно кандидатов 2, 4, 5, 6 и 7. Кандидаты 0, 1 и 3 — те же планы, что 2 и 4, только в другом масштабе; их итог должен лечь между 2 и 4.

**Что общего у всех.** Стартового запаса хватает примерно на два дня. Первые поставки приходят только на 5-й день. Поэтому за дни 0–4 любой план получает неустойки примерно на 1 060. К 3–4 дню деньги почти кончаются, и план проигрывает или выигрывает в зависимости от того, какие заказы урезаются или отменяются. Важно, что урезание идёт с товара 0. А деньги при нехватке выгоднее тратить на товар 1: он дешевле (5 против 11), а потеря от нехватки почти та же (около 15 против 16 за единицу).

**Кандидаты 0–4.** Заказ 4-го дня урезается до 10–38 единиц товара 0, товар 1 не заказывается совсем. Заказ 6-го дня урезается почти до нуля, около 5 единиц товара 0. В итоге в дни 9–12 не хватает примерно 100–123 единиц товара 1 и 44–54 единиц товара 0. Это около 2 400–2 550 упущенной прибыли.

**Кандидат 5 (ежедневные заказы).** Заказ 4-го дня урезается, 5-го отменяется (под пик спроса 47 на 10-й день), 6-го урезается до 5 единиц товара 0. Нехватка — около 47 единиц товара 0 и 69 единиц товара 1, это примерно 1 790. Сверху ещё около 390 чистых лишних расходов: двенадцать дополнительных сборов по 54 минус экономия на хранении. Всего около 2 180.

**Кандидат 6 (заказы раз в три дня).** Заказ 3-го дня урезается, заказ 6-го отменяется. В дни 9–13 не хватает около 107 единиц товара 1. Это худший вариант.

**Кандидат 7.** Тоже теряет заказ 5-го дня и часть заказа 7-го (по товару 1 примерно 68 вместо 83). Но поставки 1-го и 3-го дня у него крупные, и запас держится до 9–10 дня. Нехватка — около 51 единицы товара 0 и 44 единиц товара 1, это примерно 1 480. Сборов всего 12. После 8-го дня деньги восстанавливаются, а заказы идут с запасом около 10 % к прогнозу, что разумно при среднем множителе 1,046.

Отрыв от ближайших конкурентов — примерно 700–900. Он появляется в первые 12 дней из-за нехватки денег и почти не зависит от того, как случайный спрос отклонится от прогноза. Поэтому выбор достаточно уверенный.

I picked candidate 0. This is an estimate worked out in my head, not a simulation, so the margin over candidates 3 and 7 is uncertain.

1. **How often to order.** Each order day costs 54. Candidate 5 orders every day, about 12 more order days than the others, which adds roughly 650 in fees. Candidate 6 orders every 3 days, so its deliveries are larger. Those plus leftover stock are more likely to overflow the 152-unit warehouse. Ordering every 2 days looks like the best trade-off.
2. **How much to order.** Candidates 0–4 follow the same every-2-days schedule at different sizes. After the first two deliveries, they order these multiples of the forecast:
   - candidate 4: about 1.0×
   - candidate 1: about 1.05×
   - candidate 3: about 1.1×
   - candidate 0: about 1.15×
   - candidate 2: about 1.25×

   Candidate 7 also orders every 2 days at about 1.1×, but on the other set of days.
3. **Over- versus under-ordering.**
   - **Short is costly:** a missing unit loses its margin plus the 8 penalty, about 16 for item 0 and 15 for item 1.
   - **Extra is cheap:** a spare unit costs little more than storage, because it can still sell in the next 2-day period. Shelf life is 6 days for item 0 and 8 for item 1.
   - **True demand is higher:** actual demand averages about 1.05× the forecast.

   Together these favour ordering above the forecast, around 1.1–1.2×.
4. **Capacity limit.** At about 1.25×, candidate 2's deliveries plus leftover stock risk overflowing the warehouse, and anything over 152 units is lost after it has been paid for. At about 1.15×, candidate 0 should come close to the limit without much loss.

Candidate 0 gives the best balance of these factors.

**Ответ: кандидат 5.** Я просчитал в уме по прогнозам mu только кандидатов 4 и 5. Остальных отсеял по деньгам в первые дни, не доводя расчёт до конца.

**Главное ограничение — деньги в первые 5 дней.** Первый заказ приходит только на 5-й день. До этого продавать можно лишь стартовые 22 + 34 единицы, это около 826 выручки. Нехватка в дни 0–4 стоит около 330 неустойки в день. Поэтому планы с крупными ранними заказами уходят в минус: заказы урезаются или отменяются, а потом склад пустеет циклами.

- **Кандидаты 0–4.** Это один и тот же план «заказ раз в 2 дня», только в разном масштабе. У кандидата 4, самого маленького из них, к 4-му дню остаётся около 461. Его заказ на 4-й день урезан до 37 ед. товара 0 и 0 ед. товара 1. Дальше каждые 2 дня денег не хватает, и каждый второй заказ режется почти до нуля. Итог — около **+280**. Кандидаты 0–3 тратят в первые дни ещё больше, так что они вряд ли лучше.
- **Кандидаты 6 и 7.** Оба делают крупные заказы рано. У кандидата 7 к 5-му дню на счёте около −340, и большой заказ этого дня отменяется. У кандидата 6 к 6-му дню около −220, его заказ тоже отменяется. Те же провалы, что у планов раз в 2 дня, только сильнее.
- **Кандидат 5.** Небольшие ежедневные заказы, примерно 1,1 × прогноз спроса на день прихода. Он тоже переживает отмены в дни 4–5, 11–12 и 17–18, но выходит из них быстро. С 19-го дня склад обеспечен полностью, без нехватки и излишков. Около 25 лишних фиксированных платежей по 54 (≈1350) окупаются многократно. Итог — около **+3650**.

Это прогноз, а не точный результат: фактический спрос случаен и в среднем примерно на 4,6 % выше прогноза. Но разрыв между кандидатами 5 и 4 настолько велик, что случайность вряд ли изменит выбор.

**Choice: candidate 7.** I traced each plan by hand on forecast demand, so the profit figures below are rough.

**The cash crunch decides the result.** The starting stock of 22 and 34 units runs out on day 1. Nothing arrives until day 5, so days 1–4 bring about 1,300 in penalties. Meanwhile orders are paid upfront, so early orders hit the cash floor and get cut or cancelled. Each cut order leaves a shortage five days later, which brings penalties that cause the next cut. Profit depends mostly on whether a plan gets out of this loop.

- **Candidates 0–4** (order every two days from day 0) all get caught. By day 4 there is only about 150–460 cash left, so the day-4 order shrinks to 9–37 units of product 0 and none of product 1. After that, cuts repeat about every six days (days 6, 12, 14, 20, 22), with stockouts on days 9–12, 17–20 and 25–28.
  - Candidate 4 makes about +260 and candidate 0 about +650.
  - Candidates 1–3 spend more than candidate 4 up front and less than candidate 0, so they land in the same loop with similar results.
- **Candidate 5** (orders every day) is worse still. It pays the 54 fee 25 times, its cash goes negative by day 4, and its day-5 order is cancelled. The shortages then pile up.
- **Candidate 6** (every three days) has its day-6 and day-15 orders cancelled, which gives two long gaps with stockouts. By day 17 it recovers and ends at about +2,400.
- **Candidate 7** has a small first order (12, 21) and makes its day-3 order before the cash runs out, so that order is paid in full. Its day-5 order is cancelled and orders on days 7 and 13 are cut, but by day 15 it keeps a cash cushion after each order. From then on it orders and sells in full and ends at about **+4,600**.

**Under random demand:** the gap between candidate 7 and the rest is large, and the cause is how the orders are timed against the cash, not their size. Normal demand swings are unlikely to change the ranking. Candidate 7's lead does depend on getting out of the cash squeeze around day 15. If demand runs low then, the recovery comes later and the margin shrinks.
